title: Debugging and Error Handling
summary: Plan for things going wrong: try, catch and finally, the built-in error types, and the console and breakpoints that show you why.

lessons.title: try, catch, finally and throw
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, handle errors properly.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An **error** stops your code in its tracks. Error handling lets you plan for that. Put risky code in a `try` block (code inside curly braces `{ }`). If something goes wrong there, the `catch` block runs instead of the program crashing. The `finally` block runs either way, so it's the spot for cleanup.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A trapeze act. The `try` is the jump, the `catch` is the safety net, and `finally` is the bow at the end, fall or no fall. Where it stops: the net only catches falls during this jump. An error thrown later, in a **callback** (a function handed over to run later), misses it.

cards.title: The three parts
cards.body: `JSON.parse()` turns text into data. If the text is broken, it throws. Then `show(data)` is skipped and `catch` runs. `hideSpinner()` runs in every case. (`show`, `showMessage` and `hideSpinner` stand for your own app's functions.)

cards.title: Rules to know
items: `try` needs a `catch`, a `finally`, or both. A bare `try` is a `SyntaxError` (code JavaScript can't read).
Each part needs its own curly braces.
The **catch binding** is the name in `catch (error)`, holding the error. It's optional: `catch { }` works when you don't need the error.
The binding (like `error`) only exists inside its `catch` block.

cards.title: throw
cards.body: `throw` raises an error on purpose. The function stops at once, and JavaScript jumps to the nearest `catch`. You can throw any value, even a string. Throw an `Error` object anyway. It carries a `name`, a `message` and a **stack trace** (the list of calls that led here).

cards.title: Throwing your own error
cards.body: `new` makes a fresh object, so `new Error('Not enough money')` is an error with that `message`. 50 is more than 10, so `throw` runs and `catch` gets the error. `console.log()` prints its `name` and `message`: this logs `Error Not enough money`.

cards.title: finally gets the last word
cards.body: `finally` runs before the code moves on, even after a `return` (which hands a value back from a function). A `return` in `try` waits until `finally` is done. If `finally` has its own `return`, that value **wins**: `try` returns 1, `finally` returns 2, you get 2. It even swallows a thrown error. Keep `finally` for cleanup only.

"My `try` wraps `setTimeout`, so its errors are caught." Wrong. `setTimeout` runs its callback later, after `try` has finished. A promise you don't `await` fails later too. Fix: put the `try` inside the callback, or `await` the promise inside an `async` function.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Try it, catch it, finally tidy it.** And `throw` real `Error` objects, never bare strings.

terms.say: JavaScript's object for "something went wrong". It has a name, a message and usually a stack trace.
A block for code that might fail. If something inside it throws, JavaScript jumps straight to the catch block.
The block that runs when code in try throws. It gets the error, so you can show a message or recover.
A block that always runs after try and catch, error or not. It's the right spot for cleanup, like hiding a spinner.
A statement that raises an error on purpose. The function stops at once, and JavaScript looks for the nearest catch.
A list of the function calls that led to an error, newest first. It shows where the error happened.
The name in catch (error). It holds whatever was thrown. You can leave it out when you don't need it.
A function you hand to other code so it can call it later, like the function you pass to setTimeout.
An object that stands for a result that isn't ready yet. Later it either fulfills with a value or rejects with an error.
A keyword that pauses an async function until a promise settles. If the promise rejects, await throws, so a try around it catches the error.
Turns JSON text into real data. The text {"a": 1} becomes an object whose a is 1. Broken text makes it throw a SyntaxError.
Makes a fresh object from a class. new Error('Oops') makes a new error object whose message is 'Oops'.
The text inside an error that says what went wrong. new Error('Oops') has the message 'Oops'.
Prints values to the console so you can see them. console.log(2 + 2) prints 4.
Ends a function and hands a value back to the code that called it. A function that does return 5 gives back 5.
Runs a function later, after a wait in milliseconds. setTimeout(sayHi, 1000) runs sayHi after about one second. The rest of your code keeps going meanwhile.
A word you put before a function so it can use await inside. An async function always gives back a promise.

lessons.title: Error types and catching selectively
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, handle errors properly.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: JavaScript has a few **built-in error types**. Each one names a different kind of problem. The type tells you what went wrong before you read the message. You can also check the type in `catch`. Then you handle the errors you expect and let the rest through.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Warning lights on a car dashboard. Fuel, oil and engine each get their own light, so you know what to fix. Where it stops: these aren't separate systems. Every error type here is a special kind of `Error`. So a check for `Error` matches all of them.

cards.title: The big four
items: `ReferenceError`: a name that doesn't exist, or a `let`/`const` used before its line (the TDZ).
`TypeError`: the wrong kind of value, like calling `undefined` or reading a property of `null`. Changing a `const` too.
`SyntaxError`: code or text that can't be read, including bad input to `JSON.parse`.
`RangeError`: a value outside the allowed range, like `new Array(-1)`.

cards.title: And the rarer ones
items: `URIError`: broken web-address codes given to `decodeURI` or `decodeURIComponent`, like a lone `%`.
`EvalError`: about `eval()`. You almost never see it.
`AggregateError`: many errors in one, with an `errors` list. `Promise.any` rejects with it when every promise fails.

cards.title: Catch only what you expect
cards.body: `instanceof` asks what type a value is: `e instanceof TypeError` is `true` when `e` is a `TypeError`. Handle the error you planned for. **Rethrow** the rest with `throw e`, so it isn't silently lost.

cards.title: Your own error type
cards.body: A **custom error** is your own error type. `extends` makes a class that builds on `Error`. In the constructor (setup code for each new object), `super(message)` lets `Error` store the `message`. Set `name` yourself, or it stays `'Error'`. Here, `new ValidationError('Bad email').name` is `'ValidationError'`.

cards.title: Keep the original
cards.body: Turning a technical error into a friendlier one? Pass the original as the **cause**: `new Error('Save failed', { cause: err })`. Later, `e.cause` gives back the original error. This is ES2022, brand new when the exam was written. Older code keeps the original on a property of its own.

Checking `e instanceof Error` first matches every built-in error, because they all extend `Error`. The first `if` that's true wins, so put specific checks like `TypeError` first. And there's no `catch (TypeError e)` in JavaScript. That's Java. Use one `catch`, then `if` checks.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Reference: no such name. Type: wrong kind of thing. Range: value out of bounds. Syntax: can't read it.** Check specific types first, and rethrow the rest.

terms.say: The error for a name JavaScript can't find, or a let or const variable used before its line runs.
The error for using a value the wrong way, like calling something that isn't a function or reading a property of null.
The error for text JavaScript can't read as valid code or valid JSON, like a missing bracket.
The error for a value outside the allowed range, like asking for an array with a length of -1.
One error that holds a list of several errors. Promise.any rejects with it when every promise fails.
An operator that asks: was this object made from this class, or one that extends it? The answer is true or false.
Throwing the same error again from catch. It passes errors you can't handle up to code that can.
Your own error type, made with a class that extends Error. It lets callers tell your errors apart from others.
An option for new Error that keeps the original error inside the new one. Nothing about the first problem gets lost.
The temporal dead zone: the part of a block before a let or const line runs. Touching the variable there throws a ReferenceError.
let and const make variables. A let variable can get a new value later. A const can't: trying throws a TypeError.
The value of something that was never given a value, like a missing property. Trying to call it like a function throws a TypeError.
A value that means empty on purpose. Reading a property of null, like null.x, throws a TypeError.
Turns JSON text into real data. The text {"a": 1} becomes an object whose a is 1. Broken text makes it throw a SyntaxError.
decodeURI and decodeURIComponent turn web-address codes back into text: 'a%20b' becomes 'a b'. A broken code, like a lone %, throws a URIError.
Takes several promises and gives the first one that succeeds. If they all fail, it fails with an AggregateError that holds every reason.
Makes a class that builds on another one. class ValidationError extends Error makes a new kind of Error that keeps everything Error has.
Inside a constructor, it runs the parent class's setup first. In a class that extends Error, super(message) lets Error store the message.

lessons.title: The console and breakpoints
lessons.objective: Given code to be debugged, use the console and breakpoints.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Debugging** means finding out why code does something you didn't expect. You have two main tools. The **console** prints values while code runs. A **breakpoint** pauses the code on a line. Then you can look at every variable and walk forward one step at a time.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: The console is a trail of sticky notes your code leaves as it runs. A breakpoint is the pause button on a movie, so you can study one frame. Where it stops: a paused page is frozen for real. Timers wait until you resume, and clicks do nothing.

cards.title: Console methods
items: `console.log()` prints a value. `info`, `debug`, `warn` and `error` print too, each at a **log level** (info, warning, error) you can filter.
`console.table(rows)`: an array or object as a table.
`console.time('x')`, later `console.timeEnd('x')`: how long it took. Same label!
`console.count('x')`: how many times this line ran.
`console.group()` and `groupEnd()`: indent related lines.
`console.trace()`: the call stack that led here.

cards.title: console.assert only logs
cards.body: `console.assert` prints an error only when the condition is false. It never throws, so the code keeps running. If `qty` is -3, you see `Assertion failed: qty is negative`, then `still running`. That's why it isn't a real check.

cards.title: Breakpoints
cards.body: Click a line number in the **Sources** panel to set a breakpoint. The code pauses before that line runs. While paused, the **Scope** pane shows the variables this code can use: local ones and closure ones (from outer functions). The **Call Stack** pane shows how you got here. **Watch** tracks any expression you type.

cards.title: Breakpoint kinds
items: **Conditional**: pauses only when your expression is true.
**Logpoint**: logs a message without pausing or editing code.
**DOM change**: when the page changes. In Elements: Break on subtree, attribute or node removal.
**Event listener**: pauses in the handler for an event like `click`.
**XHR/fetch**: pauses when a request URL contains your text.
**Exceptions**: pause on thrown errors, caught or uncaught.

cards.title: Stepping and debugger
cards.body: Paused? **Step over** runs the current line, including any function it calls. **Step into** goes inside the called function. **Step out** finishes this function and pauses back in the caller. The `debugger` statement pauses like a breakpoint, but only when dev tools are open.

"A leftover `debugger;` will freeze the app for real users." No. With no debugger attached, it does nothing. Also, `console.assert` is not a test. A false assertion just prints a line, and the code keeps going.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Log to look, break to stop.** Into goes in, over goes past, out goes back.

terms.say: A panel in the browser's dev tools, or your terminal in Node, where code can print messages and values.
A marker on a line of code. When the code reaches that line, it pauses so you can look at everything.
How serious a console message is, like info, warning or error. The console can show or hide messages by level.
Prints an array or object as a neat table, one row per item. Great for lists of records.
Starts a named stopwatch. console.timeEnd with the same name stops it and prints how many milliseconds passed.
Checks a condition. If it's false, it prints an error message. It never throws, so your code keeps running.
The list of functions running right now, each called by the one below it. It shows how the code got to this line.
A breakpoint that prints a message instead of pausing. You add it in dev tools, so you don't edit the code.
A statement that pauses code like a breakpoint when dev tools are open. With no debugger attached, it does nothing.
A debugger button. On a line that calls a function, it moves inside that function and pauses there.
Prints values to the console so you can see them. console.log(2 + 2) prints 4.
Counts how many times it has run with a label, and prints it. Calling console.count('x') twice prints x: 1, then x: 2.
Starts an indented group: lines printed after it are pushed to the right. console.groupEnd() ends the group.
Prints the call stack: the chain of function calls that led to this line. It doesn't pause anything.
The browser's built-in tools for developers: the console, the debugger, the page's elements and more. In Chrome, right-click the page and pick Inspect to open them.
The page as a tree of objects that JavaScript can read and change. Each tag on the page, like a button, is a node in that tree.
A debugger button. It runs the current line, including any function that line calls, then pauses on the next line.
A debugger button. It finishes the current function, then pauses back in the code that called it.

flashcards.back: Every time, before the code moves on: after success, after a caught error, even after a `return`. A `return` inside `finally` replaces the earlier one.

flashcards.front: What must come after a `try` block?
flashcards.back: A `catch`, a `finally`, or both. A bare `try` is a `SyntaxError`. Each part must be a block in curly braces.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `try` catch an error thrown in a `setTimeout` callback?
flashcards.back: The callback runs later, after the `try` has finished. Put the `try` inside the callback, or `await` a promise inside `try`.

flashcards.front: Why throw an `Error` object instead of a string?
flashcards.back: You can throw any value, but an `Error` carries a `name`, a `message` and a stack trace that shows where it failed.

flashcards.front: Which error do you get for using a `let` variable before its line runs?
flashcards.back: `ReferenceError`. The variable is in the temporal dead zone (TDZ) until its declaration runs.

flashcards.front: Which error comes from calling `undefined` or reading a property of `null`?
flashcards.back: `TypeError`: the value is the wrong kind for what you did. Assigning to a `const` is a `TypeError` too.

flashcards.front: How do you handle just one error type in `catch` and pass the rest on?
flashcards.back: Check it with `if (e instanceof TypeError)` and handle it. Use `throw e` for everything else. Put specific checks before a check for `Error`.

flashcards.front: A class extends `Error` but never sets `name`. What is its `name`?
flashcards.back: `'Error'`. It inherits that `name` from `Error.prototype`. To change it, set `this.name = 'MyError'` in the constructor.

flashcards.front: What does `console.assert(cond, msg)` do when `cond` is false?
flashcards.back: It prints an error message to the console. It doesn't throw, so the code keeps running. It isn't a real test.

flashcards.front: How do you time a block of code with the console?
flashcards.back: `console.time('label')` before and `console.timeEnd('label')` after. The labels must match exactly, including case.
It pauses like a breakpoint when dev tools are open. With no debugger attached, it does nothing.

flashcards.front: What do step over, step into and step out do?
flashcards.back: Over runs the current line, calls included. Into goes inside the called function. Out finishes this function and pauses in the caller.

questions.q: When does a `finally` block run?
options: Every time, before control leaves the statement
Only when the `try` block throws an error
Only when the `try` block ends without any error at all
Only when the `catch` block throws again
questions.explain: `finally` always runs before the code leaves the `try` statement. It runs after success, after a caught error, and even after a `return`.
wrong: It also runs when nothing is thrown.
It also runs after an error, caught or not.
It runs whether or not `catch` throws.

questions.q: Which two snippets are a `SyntaxError`? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: A `try` needs a `catch`, a `finally`, or both, and every part must be a block in braces. A bare `try` and a `try` without braces both fail to parse.
wrong: `try` with only `finally` is a valid form.
The catch binding is optional, so `catch { }` is valid.
All three parts together is a valid form.

questions.q: What does this code log, in order?
options: Only `try`, since `finally` is skipped after a `return`
questions.explain: `finally` runs before the function really returns. So `cleanup` prints inside `f()`, then the outer `console.log` prints the returned `try`.
wrong: `f()` must finish before its result can be logged, and `finally` runs inside `f()`.
`finally` still runs after a `return`.
The `return` value isn't lost; it is handed back after `finally`.

questions.q: What happens when this code runs?
options: `after` is logged, then the error goes uncaught
`caught late` is logged, and then `after` is never reached
questions.explain: A `try` only catches errors thrown while it runs. The `setTimeout` callback runs later, outside it, so its error is uncaught. Put the `try` inside the callback instead.
wrong: The callback runs later, after the `try` statement has finished.
When the timer fires, no `catch` is around the callback anymore.
Nothing is thrown during the `try` block itself.

questions.q: A function only needs to know whether `JSON.parse` worked. It never reads the error. Which `catch` clause is valid?
questions.explain: The catch binding is optional. When you don't need the error, leave out the name and its parentheses: `catch { }`.
wrong: Empty parentheses are a `SyntaxError`. Drop them along with the binding.
`catch` must be followed by a block in braces.
The binding is fine, but the body must be a block in braces.

questions.q: Why should code throw an `Error` object instead of a plain string?
options: It carries a `name`, a `message` and a stack trace
Plain strings can't be thrown; only `Error` objects can
A thrown string skips the `finally` block
questions.explain: You can throw any value, but an `Error` object carries useful details. Its `name`, `message` and stack trace show what failed and where.
wrong: `throw` accepts any value, strings included.
`finally` runs no matter what value was thrown.
`catch` receives whatever value was thrown.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: `catch` receives exactly what was thrown. Here that is the string `'Oops'`, so `typeof e` is `'string'` and `e.length` is 4. A string has no `message` or stack trace.
wrong: Nothing wraps the string in an object or an `Error`.
`e` is the string itself, and `'Oops'` has a length of 4.
The thrown value is a plain string, not an object.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: An inner `try` with no `catch` runs its `finally`, then the error moves outward. The nearest `catch` around it handles the error.
wrong: The inner `finally` runs before control moves out to the outer `catch`.
The error keeps going after `finally` and reaches the outer `catch`.
The outer `catch` handles the error the inner `try` didn't.

questions.q: Which two statements about `finally` are true? (Choose 2)
options: It runs only when the `catch` block didn't handle the thrown error
It runs even when `try` has already reached a `return`
It can't be used on its own; a `catch` block must come before it
A `return` inside it replaces any earlier `return` value
It runs before the `try` block, to set things up
questions.explain: `finally` always runs before the code moves on, even after a `return`. If `finally` itself returns, that value replaces the earlier one.
wrong: It runs every time, handled or not.
`try...finally` is a valid form on its own.
It runs after `try` and `catch`, never before.

questions.q: A function reads a settings string from storage. Bad text must return `null` instead of crashing the page. Which body does that?
questions.explain: `JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` on bad text. Only a `try...catch` can turn that throw into a normal return value.
wrong: Bad text that isn't empty still reaches `JSON.parse` and throws.
A reviver (the second argument) only changes values after parsing. Bad text still throws.
`??` only helps with `null` or `undefined`. It can't stop a throw.

questions.q: What happens right after a `throw` statement runs?
options: The function stops, and control jumps to the nearest `catch`
The next line runs, and the error is reported later
The function restarts from its first line
The error is ignored unless `finally` is present
questions.explain: `throw` ends the current block at once. JavaScript jumps to the nearest `catch` around it, running any `finally` blocks on the way. With no `catch` at all, the error is uncaught.
wrong: Nothing after `throw` in that block runs.
Code never restarts on its own after a throw.
Without a `catch`, the error moves up to the code that called the function.

questions.q: `fetchData()` returns a promise that rejects. Callers of `load()` get the rejection instead of `'fallback'`. Which change makes the `catch` block handle it?
options: Change the line to `return await fetchData();`
Remove `async` so the promise is returned directly
questions.explain: A `try` only catches what fails while it runs. `return fetchData()` hands the promise out, and it rejects later. With `await`, the rejection throws inside the `try`, so `catch` runs.
wrong: A `return` in `finally` would replace every result, even a good one.
The binding has nothing to do with which errors are caught.
Then the rejection still happens later, outside the `try`.

questions.q: What does this code log, in order?
questions.explain: A throw inside `catch` waits until `finally` has run. Then the new error `B` leaves `run()` and reaches the outer `catch`.
wrong: `finally` inside `run()` finishes before the error leaves `run()`.
The outer `try` catches `B`.
`finally` runs even when `catch` throws.

questions.q: What does `check()` return, and what happens to the error?
options: It returns `'done'`, then the error is thrown
It throws `bad input`, and the `return` never runs
It returns `undefined`, and the error is logged
It returns `'done'`, and the error is discarded
questions.explain: A `return` in `finally` replaces whatever was about to happen. Here `return 'done'` replaces the throw, so the error silently disappears. That's why `finally` should only clean up.
wrong: A function can't both return and throw. The `return` wins.
`finally` runs before the error leaves, and its `return` replaces the throw.
The `return` in `finally` gives `'done'`, and nothing logs the error.

questions.q: `save()` returns a promise that rejects. The code logs `saved`, and the rejection shows up as unhandled. Which two changes let the code handle it? (Choose 2)
options: Add a `finally` block after the `catch` block
Wrap the whole `try` statement in a second `try`
Move it into an `async` function and use `await save();` inside `try`
questions.explain: A rejected promise doesn't throw into a plain `try`. Handle it on the promise with `.catch()`, or `await` it inside `try` in an `async` function.
wrong: `finally` can't catch anything, and the rejection still happens later.
No `try` can see a rejection that arrives after it has finished.
That moves the call outside the `try`, which helps even less.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: The `return` value is worked out first (1), then `finally` runs. `finally` raises `count` to 2 but doesn't change the value already being returned.
wrong: The return value was already worked out before `finally` ran.
`finally` still runs and adds 1 to `count`.
`count` ends at 2, and the function returned 1.

questions.q: How many times are `try` and `fin` logged?
questions.explain: `finally` runs whenever the code leaves the `try` block, also through `continue` (skip to the next turn). So `fin` logs on all 3 turns, while `try` skips turn 1.
wrong: `finally` still runs when `continue` leaves the `try` block.
When `i` is 1, `continue` skips the `console.log` in `try`.
`continue` skips a `try` log, not a `fin` log.

questions.q: Which error does the second line throw?
questions.code:
const settings = {};
settings.load();
questions.explain: Calling something that isn't a function is a `TypeError`. `settings.load` is `undefined`, and `undefined` can't be called.
wrong: `settings` exists. The problem is the kind of value, not the name.
The code parses fine. It fails while running.
No number is out of range here.

questions.q: What happens when this code runs?
questions.code:
console.log(total);
let total = 5;
options: It logs `undefined`, as hoisting moves the declaration up
questions.explain: A `let` or `const` variable is in the temporal dead zone (TDZ) until its line runs. Reading it there throws a `ReferenceError`.
wrong: That's how `var` behaves, not `let`.
The value 5 isn't stored until the `let` line runs.
Touching a `let` variable too early is a `ReferenceError`.

questions.q: A function builds `new Array(size)`. A caller passes `-1`. Which error is thrown?
questions.explain: An array length must be a whole number from 0 up. A value outside the allowed range throws a `RangeError`.
wrong: -1 is the right type (a number). Its value is out of range.
No name is missing here.
That's only for broken web-address codes given to `decodeURI` or `decodeURIComponent`.

questions.q: A developer passes three promises to `Promise.any()`, and all three reject. What does the returned promise reject with?
options: Only the first rejection reason, as it arrived
An `AggregateError` that lists all three reasons
Only the last rejection reason, as it arrived
A `RangeError`, because no promise was left
questions.explain: `Promise.any` fulfills with the first success. If every promise rejects, it rejects with an `AggregateError`, whose `errors` list holds all the reasons.
wrong: `Promise.any` waits for all of them and keeps every reason.
No single reason is picked; all are kept together.
The error type for this case is `AggregateError`.

questions.q: Which call throws a `URIError`?
questions.explain: `URIError` is for broken web-address codes. A lone `%` isn't a valid code, so `decodeURIComponent` throws.
wrong: Encoding a space is fine; it returns `'a%20b'`.
Bad JSON throws a `SyntaxError`.
`parseInt` never throws here; it returns `NaN`.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: A class that extends `Error` inherits `name` from `Error.prototype`, which is `'Error'`, unless the class sets its own. And every object it makes is also `instanceof Error`.
wrong: The class never sets `name`, so it inherits `'Error'`.
`name` isn't set, and the class does extend `Error`.
A class that extends `Error` still makes objects that are `instanceof Error`.

questions.q: Given this class, which two are true for `const e = new ValidationError('Too short')`? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: A class that extends `Error` makes objects that are `instanceof` both classes. `super(message)` stores the `message`.
wrong: The constructor sets `name` to `'ValidationError'`.
`ValidationError` extends `Error`, not `TypeError`.
`e` was made by `new ValidationError`, so it's `true`.

questions.q: Inside `catch (e)`, the code must handle a `TypeError` and pass every other error on. Which code does that?
options: `if (e instanceof TypeError) { fix(); } else { throw e; }`
questions.explain: Use `instanceof` to check the error's type. Handle the one you expect and rethrow the rest, so other errors aren't silently lost.
wrong: `e` is an error object, never the `TypeError` class itself.
`typeof` gives `'object'` for errors, never a class name.
`return` swallows the other errors instead of passing them on.

questions.q: What does this code log?
questions.explain: `JSON.parse` throws a `SyntaxError` at run time for bad text. The `instanceof SyntaxError` check matches, so `readConfig` returns `{}`.
wrong: The `catch` returns `{}`, not nothing.
Bad JSON throws a `SyntaxError`, and this `catch` handles exactly that type.
`JSON.parse` doesn't return `null` for bad text; it throws.

questions.q: What does this code log?
